body:
I guess it should also be noted that `godot_cleanup_profiler()` is now in a bit of an awkward state, since we're not actually cleaning stuff up in there anymore.

How much of a problem do we deem this to be? Should I bother making some sort of `TracyInternTable` list that we can explicitly clean up in `godot_cleanup_profiler()`?

EDIT: I went ahead and added this, since I had to fix a cleanup bug I had snuck in at the last second anyway.

I can see contention being a problem in multi-threaded applications. I was foreseeing this, but I was hoping for a different solution: allocating the needed profiling data before the call, avoiding the mutex entirely.
This would require some collaboration with the scripting API, to be able to create and link call data before the tracing call, but it would solve the multiplied memory problem _and_ the mutex problem at the same time.

A different temporary solution might be switching to an R/W lock. Write-mode locking would only be needed on first call, so once a function is registered, all reads can be simultaneous.
This would require a bit of refactoring as well, and wouldn't remove the locking overhead. But it should mitigate the multi-threading contention.

> A different temporary solution might be switching to an R/W lock. [...] But it should mitigate the multi-threading contention.

I can give it a try, but I suspect we'll just be switching out one type of contention for another, as readers claiming (and releasing) the lock typically write to some atomic within the lock. I've seen pretty terrible scaling from R/W locks when there are a lot of concurrent readers and the scope is small-ish.

> but I suspect we'll just be switching out one type of contention for another

Indeed. Here are the results from the MRP when running with [this branch](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/b7d827914d94de469e28ea2f67764ea89fc39ac0) (and `optimize=speed lto=thin`):

```
1 thread: 5329 ms
32 threads: 5525 ms
Ideal scaling (assuming hyper-threading) would be 16x, but actual scaling is 1.0x
```

So barely any better[^1] than a normal mutex. See [this explanation](https://github.com/facebook/folly/blob/5bbbdd629bfe7185c9e7985d1d36243783057117/folly/SharedMutex.h#L150-L160) in Meta's Folly library for why that is.

To work around this we would likely need to add some kind of custom "striped" R/W lock instead, where you have multiple (typically a fixed number) reader counters separated by `CACHE_LINE_BYTES` and then manage the exclusive locking with a `BinaryMutex`, which I'm guessing is along the lines of what Folly does in its `SharedMutex`.

That does still effectively cap the number of concurrent readers though, since you'll still run into cache line bouncing once the number of concurrent readers exceed the number of counters, but setting it to 128 or more should make that a non-issue for the foreseeable future I guess.

[^1]: `perf c2c` confirms that `pthread_rwlock_rdlock`/`pthread_rwlock_unlock` in `tracy::intern_source_location` is causing a lot of cache misses.

> To work around this we would likely need to add some kind of custom "striped" R/W lock instead

I guess the question I meant to ask in my last comment is whether it's worth the effort to actually do this, or if we're fine with the multiplied memory usage of this PR as a temporary solution?

I can maybe shave off a little bit of redundant memory by at least sharing the `PagedAllocator`s between all the thread-local instances, since we don't necessarily benefit much from the slow/allocating path being lockless.

Good to know - i wasn't aware that R/W locks are so costly in locking.

I think the best solution would be script involvement then: Create the needed profiler method data at method creation, which means we won't need to intern and can just use a pointer attached to the method info. Or something like that anyway. I had always expected that would be the long-term solution.

It would be a good amount of refactor though.
If your thread-local solution has acceptable memory use, and is way faster than using a mutex, I might be OK with accepting it as an interims solution.

> If your thread-local solution has acceptable memory use, and is way faster than using a mutex, I might be OK with accepting it as an interims solution.

I'll try to get some hard numbers tomorrow.

Alright, so this snowballed a bit...

I started to stress test the thread-local version of this, using a benchmark in a real-world project that was likely to touch a lot of source locations, and ran that concurrently on 16+ threads. This actually led to the Tracy client crashing, because it apparently has an undocumented (?) cap on the amount of source locations you can allocate, at ~32k total (static and dynamic combined), as you can see [here](https://github.com/wolfpld/tracy/blob/4e670fcaf5d6541d69761c60b86b9f1ad049d528/server/TracyWorker.cpp#L3385-L3389).

That obviously makes the thread-local approach quite problematic, since at 16 threads you're limited to 2k source locations per thread, which is a fairly small amount in real-world projects.

So I've just pushed the other approach I talked about, meaning the custom R/W lock, which (with some LLM assistance) turned out to not be nearly as messy as I had imagined it. I dare say it's actually readable[^1], which is a luxury with concurrency stuff.

With this new approach we obviously have very similar memory characteristics compared to the global `BinaryMutex` approach, since we're not doing any thread-local stuff anymore, but we get to keep the nearly linear scaling that we had with the thread-local approach, as you can see in this new output from the MRP:

```
1 thread: 4914 ms
32 threads: 324 ms
Ideal scaling (assuming hyper-threading) would be 16x, but actual scaling is 15.2x
```

(The scaling in our real-world benchmark similarly lines up with what you'd get without `profiler=tracy`.)

I also threw in a couple of other changes, which were:

1. `_intern_name` wasn't actually working (prior to this PR) as it compared against a hash that was never written to. I've removed the hash in favor of `_data->name == p_name` instead, since that just does a pointer comparison anyway.
2. The `prev` pointers seemed to serve no purpose, so I chose to remove them.
3. The various members are all zero-initialized now, including the fixed-size arrays.

[^1]: I say this knowing that deadlocks often hide in plain sight.

Some of the AI assistance involved in authoring this would likely not qualify as menial, as described by [the new contribution policies](https://godotengine.org/article/contribution-policy-2026/), so I'll go ahead and close this.

I still think this style of locking is a solid approach from a performance standpoint, albeit somewhat messy from a readability standpoint, but it seemed like pre-allocation was the more desirable approach anyway, so maybe it's for the best to not go down this road.

I'll see about making a separate PR for the largely unrelated changes I threw in at the end, when I can find some time to test them again.
